After the Shock

In micro, a supply curve is drawn along costs. In macro, short-run supply hangs on the prices people expected.

When prices turn out higher than expected, 🏪 shops happily produce more. Once expectations catch up, output returns to its normal place. A demand shock ends up raising only prices over time. A supply shock, like pricier 🛢️ oil, cuts output and raises prices together. As the shock fades, the economy slowly finds its way back.

For example, a snack bar 🧑 owner expects plates to sell at 3,000 won and stocks up for a normal week. A festival suddenly floods the shop, so the owner cooks late into the night. Next year the owner plans for higher prices from the start, and output is back to normal. After the busy spell, only the higher prices remain.

Oil prices jump and production costs rise — a supply shock that lifts the short-run supply curve by 222.

How do output and prices move in the first year?

Show proof

  1. The new equilibrium is Y=93.3Y = 93.3Y=93.3, P=11.33P = 11.33P=11.33.

    Output drops below its natural level while prices rise — both go the wrong way.

    That is stagflation.

  2. It looks like a supply drop in one micro market, but here the whole economy's prices and output shake together. That is the central bank's dilemma: cut rates and prices jump further; raise them and output falls further.

  3. This shock is temporary and halves every year.

    Expected prices rise for a while, then settle back, and in the end Y=100Y = 100Y=100, P=10P = 10P=10 is restored.

    Check it with the time slider.
